outcome: The classical conjecture (finitely many nonconstant irreducible integer polynomials with positive leading coefficients, no fixed prime divisor obstruction implies infinitely many simultaneous prime values) remains completely open in the window; all work found addresses variants, analogues, or problems conditional on Hypothesis H, not the stated conjecture itself.
summary: Schinzel's Hypothesis H (as stated: over Z, arbitrary finite collections of irreducible polynomials, existence of infinitely many simultaneous prime values absent a fixed-divisor obstruction) is untouched since 26 January 2024. The current Wikipedia article still states that the only proved instance is the single-linear-polynomial case (Dirichlet's theorem), and no post-2024 source contradicts this. Several genuinely new pieces of work exist in the window, but every one changes the question rather than settling a case of it, matching the triage's assessment: (1) Behajaina and Dèbes, 'Integrally Hilbertian rings and the polynomial Schinzel hypothesis' (arXiv:2502.09959, submitted 14 Feb 2025) proves a Schinzel-type statement with Z replaced by the polynomial ring Z[U] (or more generally any integrally Hilbertian ring) and 'prime' replaced by 'irreducible' — this is a different ring and a different notion of primality, a related problem rather than a restriction of the stated one; the abstract's claim of 'consequences for the classical Schinzel Hypothesis itself' refers to structural analogies, not a proof of any case over Z. (2) A 2025/2026 paper in Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society and a companion 2025 European Journal of Mathematics paper ('Towards a Schinzel-Wójcik theorem for number fields') study the Schinzel-Wójcik problem UNDER Hypothesis H as a hypothesis — i.e. they assume Hypothesis H and derive consequences about multiplicative orders, which is orthogonal to proving or bounding Hypothesis H itself. (3) A search for 'Sierpinski's Hypothesis H1' (arXiv:2512.22413, Matt Visser, Dec 2025/July 2026) turned up only because of the coincidental 'Hypothesis H' naming; it concerns a wholly unrelated conjecture of Sierpinski about primes in square arrays of consecutive integers, verified numerically to ~10 billion cases — not Schinzel's conjecture at all. (4) An unreviewed July 2024 TechRxiv preprint by Jihyeon Yoon claims a 'Proof of Bunyakovsky Conjecture' (the k=1 special case of Hypothesis H); it has no expert digestion, no arXiv listing, no citations, and TechRxiv is not a mathematics venue — this is a dead end with no evidentiary weight, not a claimed resolution. No AI system appears anywhere in any of these sources' methods or acknowledgements. I could not access the STNB2025 survey PDF (connection refused) or the Pollack finite-field explicit-approach PDF was only searched, not fully read, but both concern different settings (function fields / finite-field polynomial rings) consistent with everything else found, so this does not change the conclusion.
competing_reading: One could argue the integrally Hilbertian rings paper (arXiv:2502.09959) is a genuine 'case' of Hypothesis H rather than a variant, since it operates within a unified framework the authors say has consequences for the classical hypothesis. But the object of study (Z[U], irreducibility rather than primality) is not a restriction of the stated problem's domain (finite polynomial collections over Z, primality of integer values) — it changes the ring and the target notion, which by §3.1 makes it a related problem, not a case.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of Hypothesis H for any concrete, nontrivial finite collection of irreducible integer polynomials with k ≥ 2 (or k=1 beyond linear, e.g. resolving the n²+1 case), published or preprinted with expert engagement, would settle the classification; short of that, an explicit statement in the Behajaina-Dèbes paper's body (not just abstract puffery) that a specific case over Z itself is settled would require re-reading the full paper rather than the abstract.
